question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam was a great man with a high level of ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. intellect.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Intellect" means the power of the mind to think, reason and understand logically. (बुद्धि / मेधा) The sentence praises Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam, a scientist and the 11th President of India, so "a high level of intellect" is the only meaningful and collocationally correct filler.

◦ Correct: Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam was a great man with a high level of intellect.

• The fixed collocation is "a high level of + abstract quality" — a high level of intellect / confidence / commitment / skill.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "intelligent humour" — "intelligent" is an adjective used for a person, not for the quality of humour in this frame; the phrase does not fit "a great man with a high level of".

• Option 2 "wise boredom" is a contradiction in terms — boredom (ऊब) is never praised.

• Option 4 "clever fatigue" is meaningless; fatigue (थकान) cannot be "clever".

NOTE

• Word family: intellect (noun), intellectual (adjective/noun), intelligence (the ability to acquire and apply knowledge), intelligible (able to be understood).

• Similar SSC collocations: "a man of letters", "a man of few words", "a person of high calibre".

question:
The following sentence contains some errors. Select the option that correctly rectifies the error.

The forses that genarate conditions conduciive to crime and riiots are stronger in urban communities than in rurral areas.
option_1: The forsec that genarate conditions conduciive to crime and riots are stronger in urban communities than in rurall areas.
option_2: The forces that genereta conditions conducieve to crime and riotts are stronger in urban communities than in rural areas.
option_3: The forces that generate conditions conducive to crime and riots are stronger in urban communities than in rural areas.
option_4: The forces that genarete conditions conduciive to crime and riots are stronger in urban communities than in ruraal areas.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The forces that generate conditions conducive to crime and riots are stronger in urban communities than in rural areas.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• This is a spelling-correction item. The given sentence misspells five words. Only Option 3 spells every one of them correctly:

◦ "forses" → "forces" (शक्तियाँ / बल)

◦ "genarate" → "generate" (उत्पन्न करना)

◦ "conduciive" → "conducive" (अनुकूल; conducive to something)

◦ "riiots" → "riots" (दंगे)

◦ "rurral" → "rural" (ग्रामीण)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 still keeps the wrong forms "forsec", "genarate", "conduciive" and "rurall".

• Option 2 still keeps "genereta", "conducieve" and "riotts".

• Option 4 still keeps "genarete", "conduciive" and "ruraal".

NOTE

• Spelling keys: FOR + CES, GEN + ER + ATE, CON + DU + CIVE, RI + OTS, RU + RAL.

• "Conducive" is always followed by the preposition "to" — "an atmosphere conducive to study".

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

I found my teacher’s points casual and informal in the group discussion.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. free and easy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "free and easy" means relaxed, casual and informal; not bound by strict rules. (सहज और अनौपचारिक) It is the exact idiomatic substitute for the underlined segment "casual and informal".

◦ Correct: I found my teacher's points free and easy in the group discussion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "flesh and blood" means one's own family/relatives, or human nature (अपना सगा-संबंधी).

• Option 3 "foot the bill" means to pay the bill/expenses (खर्च उठाना).

• Option 4 "fair and square" means honestly and straightforwardly (ईमानदारी से).

NOTE

• Note the difference: "free and easy" (relaxed manner) vs "easy come, easy go" (money gained easily is lost easily).

• Other binomial idioms for SSC: "rough and ready", "part and parcel", "null and void", "by and large", "safe and sound".

question:
Select the word which means the same as the group of words given.

One who is all powerful.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Omnipotent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Omnipotent" means one who is all-powerful; having unlimited power. (सर्वशक्तिमान) The Latin roots are "omni-" (all) + "potens" (powerful).

◦ Example: Believers hold that God is omnipotent.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Omnipresent" — present everywhere at the same time (सर्वव्यापी).

• Option 3 "Optimist" — a person who looks at the bright side of things (आशावादी).

• Option 4 "Omniscient" — one who knows everything (सर्वज्ञ).

NOTE

• The "omni-" family is a favourite of SSC: omnipotent (all-powerful), omnipresent (present everywhere), omniscient (all-knowing), omnivorous (eating both plants and flesh), omnibus (a volume containing several works).

• Related pairs: optimist × pessimist; theist × atheist.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

Ramesh is owning a beautiful house in Noida.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. owns.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Own" is a stative verb (a verb of possession). Stative verbs are not used in continuous (progressive) tenses, so "is owning" is wrong; the simple present "owns" must be used.

◦ Correct: Ramesh owns a beautiful house in Noida.

• The subject "Ramesh" is third person singular, so the verb takes "-s" — owns.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "did owned" is wrong — after "did" the base form (V1) is used ("did own"), and even that is emphatic, not required here.

• Option 3 "has owning" is not a valid structure ("has owned" would be the present perfect).

• Option 4 "was owned" is a passive form and reverses the intended meaning (the house is owned, not Ramesh).

NOTE

• Common stative verbs never used in the continuous form: own, possess, belong, have (possess), know, understand, believe, like, love, hate, want, need, seem, contain, consist, resemble.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

When Nisha will have finished her task?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. When Nisha will.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In an interrogative sentence the auxiliary/helping verb must come BEFORE the subject. The correct order after the question word "When" is "will Nisha", not "Nisha will".

◦ Correct: When will Nisha have finished her task?

• Structure of a WH-question: WH-word + auxiliary + subject + main verb + object.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "have" and "finished" together form the future perfect "will have finished", which is correct.

• "her task" is the correct object.

NOTE

• Compare: "Where is he going?" (correct) / "Where he is going?" (wrong).

• Inversion is dropped only in indirect/reported questions: "Tell me when Nisha will have finished her task." (no question mark, no inversion).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

He push the bushes aside and went a little farther.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. pushed the bushes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The second verb of the sentence, "went", is in the simple past tense. By the rule of parallelism of tense, the first verb must also be in the simple past — "pushed".

◦ Correct: He pushed the bushes aside and went a little farther.

• The object "the bushes" (plural, definite) is retained unchanged; only the verb form needs correction.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "pushed with bush" changes the meaning and drops the article.

• Option 2 "pushing the bush" is a participle and leaves the clause without a finite verb.

• Option 3 "pushes in bush" is simple present and clashes with "went".

NOTE

• When two actions joined by "and" happen in the same time frame, both verbs must be in the same tense: "He opened the door and walked in."

• Note also "farther" (physical distance) vs "further" (extent/degree).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

Copying someone else’s work and trying to submit it as your own
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Plagiarism.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Plagiarism" means the act of copying another person's work, ideas or words and passing them off as one's own. (साहित्यिक चोरी)

◦ Example: The student's thesis was rejected for plagiarism.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Polygamy" — the practice of having more than one spouse at a time (बहुविवाह).

• Option 3 "Preamble" — an introductory statement, e.g., the Preamble to the Constitution (प्रस्तावना).

• Option 4 "Extempore" — a speech delivered without previous preparation (तत्काल / बिना तैयारी).

NOTE

• Related words: plagiarise (verb), plagiarist (the person).

• Other marriage-related one-word substitutes: monogamy (one spouse), bigamy (two spouses), polyandry (many husbands), polygyny (many wives), celibacy (abstaining from marriage).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Beauty of it
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Good points.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "the beauty of it" is used to point out the best or most advantageous feature of something — its good points. (सबसे अच्छी बात यह है कि …)

◦ Example: The scheme is cheap, and the beauty of it is that anyone can join.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Make things worse" corresponds to the idiom "add fuel to the fire" / "to make matters worse".

• Option 2 "Cause for dispute" corresponds to "bone of contention" / "apple of discord".

• Option 3 "Quite ordinary" corresponds to "run of the mill" / "nothing to write home about".

NOTE

• Related expressions: "beauty is in the eye of the beholder" (beauty is a matter of personal taste), "beauty is only skin deep" (outer looks are not what really matter).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.

The girl was manacled and locked in the room.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. fettered.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Manacled" means handcuffed; bound with chains or shackles. (हथकड़ी लगाना / बेड़ियों में जकड़ना) Its closest synonym is "fettered", which means chained or shackled (especially by the feet), and hence restrained.

◦ Example: The prisoner was manacled/fettered before being taken to court.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "unfastened" (untied/loosened) and Option 2 "liberated" (set free) are antonyms.

• Option 4 "unbinded" is not a word at all; the correct form would be "unbound".

NOTE

• Synonyms of manacled: fettered, shackled, handcuffed, chained, bound, restrained.

• Antonyms: freed, released, liberated, unshackled, unfettered.

• Noun forms: a manacle is a handcuff; a fetter is a leg-iron. Figuratively, "the fetters of tradition" means its restrictions.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.

Addiction of drugs proved detrimental for his health.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Beneficial.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Detrimental" means harmful; causing damage or injury. (हानिकारक) Its exact antonym is "beneficial", meaning helpful or advantageous. (लाभदायक)

◦ Example: Smoking is detrimental to health, whereas exercise is beneficial.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Impartial" — unbiased, fair (निष्पक्ष).

• Option 2 "Potential" — possible/latent capacity (संभावित).

• Option 4 "Differential" — relating to a difference (विभेदक).

These three are unrelated to "harmful" and are only sound-alike distractors.

NOTE

• Synonyms of detrimental: harmful, injurious, damaging, deleterious, adverse, prejudicial.

• Antonyms: beneficial, advantageous, helpful, favourable, salutary.

• Usage: "detrimental to health" is the standard preposition.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Plunge
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Dive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Plunge" means to jump or dive suddenly into water; to fall/throw oneself steeply downward. (गोता लगाना / अचानक गिरना) Its closest synonym is "dive".

◦ Example: He plunged/dived into the river to save the child.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Transgress" — to break a law or moral rule (उल्लंघन करना).

• Option 3 "Rush" — to move hurriedly; it conveys speed but not the downward/into-water sense.

• Option 4 "Fly" — to move through the air, the opposite direction of a plunge.

NOTE

• Synonyms of plunge: dive, submerge, immerse, nosedive, plummet, descend.

• Antonyms: rise, ascend, soar, emerge.

• "Plunge" is also used figuratively: "share prices plunged", "the country was plunged into crisis", "take the plunge" (to decide to do something risky at last).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Tomatos.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Tomatos" is misspelt. The correct plural of "tomato" is "tomatoes" (टमाटर). Nouns ending in a consonant + o normally take "-es" in the plural.

◦ Correct: potato → potatoes, tomato → tomatoes, hero → heroes, mango → mangoes, echo → echoes, volcano → volcanoes.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "Weather" (the state of the atmosphere — मौसम), "Vehicle" (a means of transport — वाहन) and "Professor" (a senior university teacher — प्राध्यापक) are all correctly spelt.

NOTE

• Words ending in a vowel + o simply add "-s": radio → radios, studio → studios, bamboo → bamboos, zoo → zoos.

• Musical terms also take only "-s": piano → pianos, photo → photos, solo → solos.

• Do not confuse the homophones weather (मौसम), whether (conjunction — क्या/चाहे) and wether (a castrated ram).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can rectify the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to rectify it, select ‘no rectification needed’.

I used a variety of sources to find the more cheap flight.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. cheapest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "More cheap" is grammatically wrong. "Cheap" is a one-syllable adjective, so its degrees are formed with "-er / -est", never with "more/most":

◦ cheap (positive) – cheaper (comparative) – cheapest (superlative).

• Here the speaker searched "a variety of sources", i.e., compared more than two options, and the definite article "the" precedes the blank. "the + superlative" is the required structure, so "the cheapest flight" is correct.

◦ Correct: I used a variety of sources to find the cheapest flight.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is wrong because the segment definitely needs rectification.

• Option 2 "cheaper" is the comparative and would need a "than" clause or a comparison between exactly two flights; it does not suit "the ... flight" after searching many sources.

• Option 4 "cheap" (positive degree) cannot follow "the" in this comparison-based sentence.

NOTE

• Degree rules: one-syllable and many two-syllable adjectives take -er/-est (tall–taller–tallest, cheap–cheaper–cheapest); longer adjectives take more/most (beautiful – more beautiful – most beautiful).

• A double comparative/superlative such as "more cheaper" or "most cheapest" is always incorrect.

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.

All the members of my family are planning to visit Jammu and Kashmir this Novembur.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Novembur.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Novembur" is misspelt. The correct spelling of the eleventh month is "November" — the last syllable is "-ber", not "-bur". (नवंबर)

◦ Correct: All the members of my family are planning to visit Jammu and Kashmir this November.

• Spelling key: NO + VEM + BER.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "Planning" (double "n" because "plan" ends in a single vowel + single consonant and the stress is on the last syllable), "Visit" and "Members" are all spelt correctly.

NOTE

• The four "-ber" months: September, October, November, December. Names of months always begin with a capital letter.

• Doubling rule: plan → planning, stop → stopping, begin → beginning; but visit → visiting, open → opening (stress not on the last syllable).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

Ravi will go to the England.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. the England.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The definite article "the" is NOT used before the names of most countries, and England is one of them. So "the England" is wrong; it must simply be "England".

◦ Correct: Ravi will go to England.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "Ravi" (proper noun subject), "will" (future auxiliary) and "go to" (verb + preposition of direction) are all correct.

NOTE

• "The" is used with country names that are plural, or that contain words like Republic/Kingdom/States: the Netherlands, the Philippines, the USA, the UK, the UAE, the Maldives.

• "The" is also used with rivers (the Ganga), oceans (the Pacific), mountain ranges (the Himalayas), deserts (the Thar) and holy books (the Ramayana), but NOT with single mountains (Mount Everest) or single islands.

question:
Select the most appropriate response in the given situation of the eve of a battle to fill in the blank.

The commander: “Honourable Emperor, all the troops have lined up for the battle and are awaiting your orders.” Emperor Chandragupta Maurya: “______________________.”
option_2: You should learn how to talk to an emperor.
option_4: We are ready for the pilgrimage.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. We will march at dawn.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• This is a situation-based / conversational response question. The commander reports that the troops have lined up for battle and await orders; therefore the Emperor's reply must be an order relating to the battle.

• "We will march at dawn" is a clear, appropriate military command — the army will advance at daybreak. (हम भोर में कूच करेंगे)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "You should learn how to talk to an emperor" is a rude rebuke; the commander has already addressed him respectfully as "Honourable Emperor", so there is nothing to object to.

• Option 3 "We will be playing cards" is frivolous and totally out of place on the eve of a battle.

• Option 4 "We are ready for the pilgrimage" is irrelevant — a pilgrimage (तीर्थयात्रा) has nothing to do with a battle.

NOTE

• In such items, always ask: (i) who is speaking, (ii) to whom, and (iii) what tone the situation demands (formal, polite, commanding, apologetic).

• Static link: Chandragupta Maurya (c. 322–298 BCE) founded the Mauryan Empire with the guidance of Chanakya (Kautilya), the author of the Arthashastra.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.

We prefer going to movies once in a blue moon.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Very rarely.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "once in a blue moon" means very rarely; hardly ever. (कभी-कभार / बहुत कम)

◦ Example: He visits his home town once in a blue moon.

• The phrase comes from the astronomical "blue moon" — the second full moon in a single calendar month, which is an uncommon event.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 4 "Very often" is the exact opposite of the idiom's meaning.

• Option 2 "Very amazingly" and Option 3 "Very diligently" (with great care and effort) have no connection with frequency.

NOTE

• Idioms of rarity: "once in a blue moon", "few and far between", "at long intervals".

• Idioms of frequency: "every now and then", "time and again", "day in and day out", "more often than not".

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.

My father told me / that in his childhood / he was walking / to school every day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. he was walking.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "every day" shows a repeated, habitual action in the past. A habit in the past is expressed by the simple past ("walked") or by "used to walk", never by the past continuous.

◦ Correct: My father told me that in his childhood he walked (or used to walk) to school every day.

• The past continuous "was walking" describes an action in progress at a particular past moment, which contradicts "every day".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "My father told me" is correct (told + indirect object).

• "that in his childhood" correctly introduces the reported clause with an adverbial of time.

• "to school every day" is correct — "school" takes no article when it refers to the institution/activity.

NOTE

• Reported speech: when the reporting verb is in the past ("told"), the reported verb also shifts to the past — present simple → past simple.

• "Used to + V1" is the classic marker of a discontinued past habit: "He used to smoke, but he doesn't now."

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the given sentence.

Today’s question paper felt like a cakewalk.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Very easy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a cakewalk" (also "a piece of cake") means something very easy to do; an effortless task. (बहुत आसान काम)

◦ Correct sense: Today's question paper felt very easy.

• The expression comes from a 19th-century dance contest in which a cake was the prize — the winner simply had to "walk" gracefully.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Options 1 "Very sweet" and 2 "Very tasty" are literal traps based on the word "cake"; idioms are never taken literally.

• Option 4 "Very difficult" is the opposite meaning.

NOTE

• Idioms meaning "easy": a piece of cake, a cakewalk, child's play, as easy as ABC, a walk in the park, plain sailing.

• Idioms meaning "difficult": a hard nut to crack, an uphill task, a tall order, no bed of roses.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

Modern football (1)________in Britain in the 19th century. Since before medieval times, ‘folk football’ games had been played in towns and villages according to local customs and with a (2)_______of rules. Industrialisation and (3)________, which reduced the amount of leisure time and space available to the working class, combined with a history of legal prohibitions against particularly (4)________ and destructive forms of folk football to undermine the game’s status from the early 19th century onward. However, football was taken up as a winter game between residence houses at public (independent) schools such as Winchester, Charterhouse and Eton. Each school had its own rules; some allowed limited handling of the ball and others did not. The (5)_________in rules made it difficult for public schoolboys entering university to continue playing except with former schoolmates.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. originated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Originate" means to begin; to come into existence; to have its source in a place. (उत्पन्न होना / आरंभ होना) The passage traces the beginning of modern football in Britain in the 19th century.

◦ Correct: Modern football originated in Britain in the 19th century.

• The whole paragraph then describes how the game developed from folk football — a beginning, not an end.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "terminated" means ended/stopped — the opposite of what the passage says.

• Option 2 "culminated" means reached its highest point/climax, and normally takes "in" a final result, not a starting point.

• Option 4 "fragmented" means broke into pieces, which does not fit "in Britain in the 19th century".

NOTE

• Synonyms of originate: begin, arise, stem from, emanate, spring up, commence.

• Word family: origin (noun), original (adjective), originality (noun), originator (one who starts something).

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

Modern football (1)________in Britain in the 19th century. Since before medieval times, ‘folk football’ games had been played in towns and villages according to local customs and with a (2)_______of rules. Industrialisation and (3)________, which reduced the amount of leisure time and space available to the working class, combined with a history of legal prohibitions against particularly (4)________ and destructive forms of folk football to undermine the game’s status from the early 19th century onward. However, football was taken up as a winter game between residence houses at public (independent) schools such as Winchester, Charterhouse and Eton. Each school had its own rules; some allowed limited handling of the ball and others did not. The (5)_________in rules made it difficult for public schoolboys entering university to continue playing except with former schoolmates.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. minimum.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage says folk football was played "according to local customs" — that is, informally, with hardly any codified regulations. Hence it was played "with a minimum of rules", i.e., with very few rules. (न्यूनतम नियमों के साथ)

◦ Correct: ... played in towns and villages according to local customs and with a minimum of rules.

• "A minimum of + noun" is a standard English structure meaning "as little as possible / very little".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 4 "maximum" contradicts the informal, customary nature of folk football.

• Option 1 "optimum" (the most favourable amount) does not suit a game that had no fixed code at all.

• Option 2 "variance" is the answer to blank no. 5, where the passage explicitly contrasts different school rules; in blank 2 the point is the scarcity, not the difference, of rules.

NOTE

• Related expressions: "a minimum of fuss", "keep costs to a minimum", "the bare minimum".

• Antonym pair for SSC: minimum (least) × maximum (greatest); minimise × maximise.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

Modern football (1)________in Britain in the 19th century. Since before medieval times, ‘folk football’ games had been played in towns and villages according to local customs and with a (2)_______of rules. Industrialisation and (3)________, which reduced the amount of leisure time and space available to the working class, combined with a history of legal prohibitions against particularly (4)________ and destructive forms of folk football to undermine the game’s status from the early 19th century onward. However, football was taken up as a winter game between residence houses at public (independent) schools such as Winchester, Charterhouse and Eton. Each school had its own rules; some allowed limited handling of the ball and others did not. The (5)_________in rules made it difficult for public schoolboys entering university to continue playing except with former schoolmates.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. urbanisation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Urbanisation" means the growth of towns and cities and the movement of people from villages into them. (शहरीकरण) The passage says the process "reduced the amount of leisure time and space available to the working class" — exactly what industrialisation and urbanisation together did in 19th-century Britain.

◦ Correct: Industrialisation and urbanisation, which reduced the amount of leisure time and space available to the working class ...

• "Industrialisation and urbanisation" is a standard collocation in social history.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "normalisation" (making something normal/standard) and Option 3 "standardisation" (making things uniform) would not reduce space for the working class.

• Option 4 "implementation" (putting a plan into effect) is incomplete without an object and makes no sense here.

NOTE

• Static link: The Industrial Revolution in Britain (c. 1760–1840) caused mass migration to factory towns, overcrowding and the loss of open commons where folk football had been played.

• Related terms: urban (of a city), rural (of the countryside), suburban (of the outskirts), metropolis (a very large city).

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

Modern football (1)________in Britain in the 19th century. Since before medieval times, ‘folk football’ games had been played in towns and villages according to local customs and with a (2)_______of rules. Industrialisation and (3)________, which reduced the amount of leisure time and space available to the working class, combined with a history of legal prohibitions against particularly (4)________ and destructive forms of folk football to undermine the game’s status from the early 19th century onward. However, football was taken up as a winter game between residence houses at public (independent) schools such as Winchester, Charterhouse and Eton. Each school had its own rules; some allowed limited handling of the ball and others did not. The (5)_________in rules made it difficult for public schoolboys entering university to continue playing except with former schoolmates.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. violent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is joined by "and" to the adjective "destructive", so the missing word must also be an adjective with a similar negative sense. "Violent" (using or involving physical force intended to hurt — हिंसक) pairs naturally with "destructive".

◦ Correct: ... legal prohibitions against particularly violent and destructive forms of folk football ...

• It also explains why laws prohibited those forms of the game.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Options 1 "traces" and 2 "undercurrents" are nouns and cannot stand parallel to the adjective "destructive".

• Option 3 "calm" is an adjective but has the opposite sense — nobody bans a game for being calm.

NOTE

• Rule of parallelism: words joined by "and" must belong to the same grammatical class (adjective + adjective, noun + noun, verb + verb).

• Collocations: "violent and destructive", "swift and decisive", "rough and tumble".

• Historical note: medieval folk football was so rough that English monarchs, including Edward II (1314), issued proclamations banning it.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

Modern football (1)________in Britain in the 19th century. Since before medieval times, ‘folk football’ games had been played in towns and villages according to local customs and with a (2)_______of rules. Industrialisation and (3)________, which reduced the amount of leisure time and space available to the working class, combined with a history of legal prohibitions against particularly (4)________ and destructive forms of folk football to undermine the game’s status from the early 19th century onward. However, football was taken up as a winter game between residence houses at public (independent) schools such as Winchester, Charterhouse and Eton. Each school had its own rules; some allowed limited handling of the ball and others did not. The (5)_________in rules made it difficult for public schoolboys entering university to continue playing except with former schoolmates.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. variance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Variance" means difference or divergence between things. (भिन्नता / मतभेद) The previous sentence states that "Each school had its own rules; some allowed limited handling of the ball and others did not" — that is, the rules differed. Hence "the variance in rules" made joint play difficult.

◦ Correct: The variance in rules made it difficult for public schoolboys entering university to continue playing except with former schoolmates.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "grouse" means a complaint/to grumble (and also a game bird) — it does not explain the difficulty.

• Option 2 "grunt" is a low guttural sound made by a person or a pig.

• Option 4 "control" would suggest regulation, but uniform control would have made joint play easier, not harder.

NOTE

• Word family: vary (verb), various/variable (adjectives), variety, variation, variance (nouns).

• Useful phrase: "at variance with" = in disagreement or conflict with. "His statement is at variance with the facts."

• Static link: The differing school codes led to the founding of The Football Association (FA) in 1863, which finally standardised the laws of the game.
